Marcus Crassus, about to make war on the Parthians, crossed the river Euphrates, and, defeated in battle, in which his son too fell, when he had withdrawn the remnants of his army onto a hill, was summoned to a parley by the enemy, who pretended that they would treat of peace, whose leader was Surenas; and being seized and resisting, that he might suffer nothing while alive, he was killed.
107. Gaius Caesar, the Treveri in Gaul being conquered, crossed a second time into Germany; and finding there no enemy, returning into Gaul, he conquered the Eburones and other states which had conspired, and pursued Ambiorix in his flight. The body of Publius Clodius, killed by Titus Annius Milo, candidate for the consulship, on the Appian Way near Bovillae, was burned by the plebs in the senate-house. When there were seditions among the candidates for the consulship — Hypsaeus, Scipio, Milo — who contended with arms and violence, to suppress these Gnaeus Pompeius . . . and was made consul for the third time by the Senate in his absence and alone, which had happened to no other. An inquiry being decreed concerning the death of Publius Clodius, Milo was condemned in court and driven into exile. A law was passed that account be taken of Caesar in his absence in his canvass for the consulship, Marcus Cato being unwilling and speaking against it. Besides this, the book contains operations carried on by Gaius Caesar against the Gauls, who almost all revolted under the leadership of Vercingetorix the Arvernian, and the laborious sieges of cities, among them Avaricum of the Bituriges and Gergovia of the Arverni.
108. Gaius Caesar conquered the Gauls at Alesia and received in surrender all the states of Gaul that had been in arms. Gaius Cassius, quaestor of Marcus Crassus, cut down the Parthians who had crossed into Syria. In his canvass for the consulship Marcus Cato suffered a repulse, Servius Sulpicius and Marcus Marcellus being created consuls. Gaius Caesar subdued the Bellovaci with other peoples of the Gauls. Besides this, the book contains the contentions among the consuls concerning sending a successor to Gaius Caesar, the consul Marcus Marcellus moving in the Senate that Caesar come to canvass for the consulship in person, when by a law passed he was to hold the provinces until the time of his consulship; and operations carried on by Marcus Bibulus in Syria.
109. The causes and beginnings of the civil war are reported, and the contentions concerning sending a successor to Gaius Caesar, who said he would not disband his armies unless they were also disbanded by Pompeius. And it contains the proceedings of Gaius Curio, tribune of the plebs, first against Caesar, then for Caesar. When a decree of the Senate had been made that a successor be sent to Caesar, and Marcus Antonius and Quintus Cassius, tribunes of the plebs, because they were hindering that decree by their vetoes, had been driven from the city . . . and it was entrusted by the Senate to the consuls and Gnaeus Pompeius to see that the commonwealth take no harm. Gaius Caesar, about to pursue his enemies in war, came with an army into Italy, took Corfinium with Lucius Domitius and Publius Lentulus and let them go, and drove Gnaeus Pompeius and the rest of his party out of Italy.

title: Ab Urbe Condita (Periochae)
text:
110. Gaius Caesar besieged Massilia, which had closed its gates; and leaving his legates Gaius Trebonius and Decimus Brutus to besiege that city, he set out for Spain, received in surrender at Ilerda Lucius Afranius and Marcus Petreius, legates of Gnaeus Pompeius, with seven legions, and let them all go unharmed, Varro too, a legate of Pompeius, being reduced into his power with his army. He gave citizenship to the people of Gades. The Massiliotes, defeated in two naval battles, after a long siege surrendered themselves to the power of Caesar. Gaius Antonius, legate of Caesar, after conducting operations badly against the Pompeians in Illyricum, was captured; in which war the men of Opitergium, beyond the Po, auxiliaries of Caesar, their raft being hemmed in by the ships of the enemy, rather than come into the power of the enemy, fell upon one another and died. Gaius Curio, legate of Caesar in Africa, when he had fought successfully against Varus, leader of the Pompeian party, was cut down with his army by Juba, king of Mauretania. Gaius Caesar crossed into Greece.
111. The praetor Marcus Caelius Rufus, when he was stirring up seditions in the city, the plebs being solicited by the hope of cancelling debts, was, his office being annulled, driven from the city and joined himself to the exile Milo, who had gathered an army of runaways. Both, while they were setting on foot war, were killed. Cleopatra, queen of Egypt, was driven from her kingdom by her brother Ptolemy. On account of the avarice and cruelty of the praetor Quintus Cassius, the people of Corduba in Spain, with two Varronian legions, fell away from the party of Caesar. Gnaeus Pompeius, besieged at Dyrrachium by Caesar, and the garrisons of Caesar being stormed with great loss to the opposing party, was freed from the siege; and the war being transferred into Thessaly, he was defeated in line at Pharsalus. Cicero remained in the camp, a man born for anything rather than war. And Caesar pardoned all of the opposing party who had committed themselves to the power of the victor.
112. The trepidation and flight of the conquered party into the different parts of the world are reported. Gnaeus Pompeius, when he had made for Egypt, by order of King Ptolemy, his ward, at the instigation of his tutor Theodotus, whose authority with the king was great, and of Pothinus, was killed by Achillas, to whom that crime had been delegated, in a small boat, before he disembarked. His wife Cornelia and his son Sextus Pompeius fled to Cyprus. Caesar, following after three days, when Theodotus had offered him the head and ring of Pompeius, was incensed and wept; . . . and he entered the tumultuous Alexandria without danger. Caesar, created dictator, brought Cleopatra back into the kingdom of Egypt, and conquered Ptolemy, who was making war on him at the instigation of the same men who had killed Pompeius, with great peril to himself. Ptolemy, while he fled, sank in his boat in the Nile. Besides this, the book contains the laborious march of Marcus Cato in Africa, through the deserts with his legions, and the war waged with little success by Gnaeus Domitius against Pharnaces.
113. The Pompeian party in Africa being strengthened, the command of it was conferred on Publius Scipio, Cato, to whom it was offered on equal terms, yielding. And when there was deliberation about destroying the city of Utica on account of the favour of its people towards Caesar, and Marcus Cato had prevailed that this be not done, Juba urging that it be destroyed, the guardianship and watch of it was entrusted to Cato. Gnaeus Pompeius, son of the Great, in Spain, having gathered forces, the leadership of which neither Afranius nor Petreius wished to undertake, renewed the war against Caesar. Pharnaces, son of Mithridates, king of Pontus, was conquered without any delay of war. When seditions had been stirred up at Rome by Publius Dolabella, tribune of the plebs, who brought a law concerning the cancelling of debts, and on that account the plebs was in tumult, soldiers being led into the city by Marcus Antonius, master of the horse, eight hundred of the plebs were cut down. Caesar gave discharge to the veterans, who demanded it with mutiny; and when he had crossed into Africa, he fought with great peril against the forces of King Juba.

title: Ab Urbe Condita (Periochae)
text:
114. Caecilius Bassus, a Roman knight of the Pompeian party, stirred up war in Syria, being abandoned by the legion of Sextus Caesar, which had gone over to Bassus, and Sextus being killed. Caesar conquered the praetor Scipio and Juba at Thapsus, their camps being stormed. Cato, having heard the news, when he had struck himself at Utica, and was being tended, his son intervening, in the very midst of the tending tore open his wound and expired, in the forty-eighth year of his age. Petreius killed Juba and himself. Publius Scipio, surrounded on his ship, added a word also to an honourable death: for when the enemy asked for the commander, he said, "The commander is well." Faustus and Afranius were killed. To the son of Cato pardon was given. Brutus, legate of Caesar in Gaul, conquered the rebelling Bellovaci in battle.
115. Caesar held four triumphs, over Gaul, over Egypt, over Pontus, over Africa, and gave a banquet and spectacles of every kind. To Marcus Marcellus, a man of consular rank, the Senate asking it, he granted return; which kindness of his Marcellus could not enjoy, being killed at Athens by Gnaeus Magius, his own client. He conducted a census, in which a hundred and fifty thousand citizens were registered. Setting out for Spain against Gnaeus Pompeius, after many expeditions on both sides and several cities stormed, he won the crowning victory with great peril at the city of Munda. . . . Pompeius; Sextus escaped.
116. Caesar held his fifth triumph, from Spain. And when very many and very great honours had been decreed him by the Senate — among them that he be called Father of the Fatherland and be sacrosanct and dictator in perpetuity — they furnished a cause of resentment against him: because, when the Senate offered him these honours while he sat before the temple of Venus Genetrix, he did not rise; and because, when the diadem placed upon his head by Marcus Antonius the consul, his colleague, while he ran among the Luperci, he set back into the seat; and because, when the tribunes of the plebs Epidius Marullus and Caesetius Flavus were stirring up resentment against him as one aiming at kingship, their power was annulled. For these reasons a conspiracy was formed against him, whose heads were Marcus Brutus and Gaius Cassius, and from Caesar's own party Decimus Brutus and Gaius Trebonius, and he was killed in the senate-house of Pompeius with twenty-three wounds, and the Capitol was occupied by his murderers. Then, oblivion of his murder being decreed by the Senate, hostages for their children being received from Antonius and Lepidus, the conspirators came down from the Capitol. By Caesar's will, Gaius Octavius, grandson of his sister, was instituted heir to one half and adopted into his name. When Caesar's body was being carried to the Campus Martius, it was burned by the plebs before the Rostra. The honour of the dictatorship was abolished forever. Chamates, a man of the lowest sort, who gave himself out to be a son of Gaius Marius, when he was stirring up seditions among the credulous plebs, was put to death.
117. Gaius Octavius came to Rome from Epirus (for thither Caesar had sent him in advance, being about to wage war in Macedonia), and being received with prosperous omens, he assumed the name of Caesar. In the confusion and tumult of affairs, Marcus Lepidus seized the chief pontificate. And when Marcus Antonius the consul was tyrannising without restraint, and had carried by violence a law concerning the exchange of provinces, and had treated with great wrongs Caesar also, who asked him to aid him against the murderers of his uncle, Caesar, about to prepare strength for himself and for the commonwealth against him, roused the veterans settled in the colonies. The fourth and the Martian legions also carried their standards from Antonius to Caesar. Then several others too, on account of the savagery of Marcus Antonius, who was slaughtering everywhere in his camp those who were suspected by him, fell away to Caesar. Decimus Brutus, to oppose Antonius who was seeking Cisalpine Gaul, occupied Mutina with an army. Besides this, the book contains the rushing about of the men of both parties to take possession of provinces, and the preparation of war.

title: Ab Urbe Condita (Periochae)
text:
118. Marcus Brutus in Greece, under the pretext of the commonwealth and of the war undertaken against Marcus Antonius, reduced into his power the army which Publius Vatinius commanded, together with the province. To Gaius Caesar, who as a private citizen had taken up arms for the commonwealth, command as propraetor was given by the Senate, with the ornaments of consular rank, and it was added that he should be a senator. Marcus Antonius besieged Decimus Brutus at Mutina; and envoys sent to him by the Senate concerning peace availed little to compose it. The Roman people put on the soldier's cloak. Marcus Brutus in Epirus subdued the praetor Gaius Antonius with his army to his power.
119. Gaius Trebonius in Asia was killed by the treachery of Publius Dolabella. On account of that crime Dolabella was judged an enemy by the Senate. When the consul Pansa had fought badly against Antonius, the consul Aulus Hirtius, coming up with an army and routing the forces of Marcus Antonius, made equal the fortune of both parties. Then Antonius, defeated by Hirtius and Caesar, fled into Gaul and joined to himself Marcus Lepidus with the legions which were under him; and he was judged an enemy by the Senate, together with all who were within his garrisons. Aulus Hirtius, who after the victory had fallen in the very camp of the enemy, and Gaius Pansa, who died of the wound he had received in the unsuccessful battle, were buried in the Campus Martius. Towards Gaius Caesar, who alone of the three leaders survived, the Senate was insufficiently grateful; for, having decreed the honour of a triumph to Decimus Brutus, freed from the siege of Mutina by Caesar, it made too ungrateful mention of Caesar and his soldiers. On account of which Gaius Caesar, his goodwill with Marcus Antonius being reconciled through Marcus Lepidus, came to Rome with an army; and those who were hostile to him being dismayed by his arrival, when he was nineteen years of age, he was created consul.
120. The consul Gaius Caesar carried a law concerning the holding of an inquiry against those by whose agency his father had been killed; and, prosecuted under that law, Marcus Brutus, Gaius Cassius, and Decimus Brutus were condemned in their absence. When Asinius Pollio also and Munatius Plancus, joined with their armies, had increased the strength of Marcus Antonius, Decimus Brutus, whom the Senate had charged to pursue Antonius, abandoned by his legions, by order of Antonius, into whose power he had come, fleeing, was cut down and killed by Capenus the Sequanian. Gaius Caesar made peace with Antonius and Lepidus on these terms, that there should be three men for setting in order the commonwealth for five years — himself and Lepidus and Antonius — and that each should proscribe his own enemies. In which proscription there were very many Roman knights, and the names of a hundred and thirty senators, and among them Lucius Paulus, brother of Marcus Lepidus, and Lucius Caesar, uncle of Antonius, and Marcus Cicero. Of him, killed by Popillius, a legionary soldier, when he was sixty-three years old, the head too, with the right hand, was set up on the Rostra. Besides this, the book contains operations carried on by Marcus Brutus in Greece.
121. Gaius Cassius, who had been charged by the Senate to pursue in war Dolabella, judged an enemy, aided by the authority of the commonwealth, reduced into his power Syria with the three armies that were in that province, and forced Dolabella, besieged in the city of Laodicea, to die. By the order of Marcus Brutus too, Gaius Antonius was captured and killed.

title: Ab Urbe Condita (Periochae)
text:
122. Marcus Brutus conducted operations with little success against the Thracians; and all the provinces and armies across the sea being reduced into his power and that of Gaius Cassius, both met at Smyrna to settle their plans for the coming war. By common counsel they pardoned the brother of Marcus Messala Publicola, who had been put in chains.
123. Sextus Pompeius, son of the Great, having gathered from Epirus the proscribed and the runaways, with an army for a long time, without possession of any place, plundering on the sea, occupied first the town of Messana in Sicily, then the whole province; and, the praetor Pompeius Bithynicus being killed, he conquered Quintus Salvidienus, legate of Caesar, in a naval battle. Caesar and Antonius crossed into Greece with their armies, about to wage war against Brutus and Cassius. Quintus Cornificius in Africa conquered in battle Titus Sextius, leader of the Cassian party.
124. Gaius Caesar and Antonius at Philippi fought with varying outcome against Brutus and Cassius, so that the right wing of each conquered, and the camp also was stormed on both sides by those who had conquered. But the death of Cassius made the fortune of the parties unequal; for, having been in that wing which had been routed, thinking the whole army routed, he took his own life. Then on the next day Marcus Brutus, defeated, also ended his life, having entreated Strato, the companion of his flight, to drive the sword into him. He was about forty years old . . . among whom Quintus Hortensius was killed.
125. Caesar, leaving Antonius across the sea — for the provinces situated in that part of the empire had fallen to him — returned into Italy and divided lands among the veterans. The mutinies of his army, which the soldiers, corrupted by Fulvia, wife of Marcus Antonius, had stirred up against their commander, he restrained with grave peril. Lucius Antonius the consul, brother of Marcus Antonius, the same Fulvia counselling, made war on Caesar. Having received into his party the peoples whose lands had been assigned to the veterans, and Marcus Lepidus, who was in charge of the guard of the city with an army, being routed, he burst into the city as an enemy.
126. Caesar, when he was twenty-three years old, besieged Lucius Antonius in the town of Perusia, and, after he had several times tried to break out and been repulsed, forced him by hunger to come into surrender, and pardoned him and all his soldiers, and razed Perusia. And all the armies of the opposing party being reduced into his power, he finished the war without any bloodshed.
127. The Parthians, under the leadership of Labienus, who had been of the Pompeian party, burst into Syria; and, Decidius Saxa, legate of Marcus Antonius, being conquered, they occupied all that province. Marcus Antonius, when to wage war against Caesar . . . his wife Fulvia, that she might not stand in the way of the concord of the leaders, peace being made with Caesar, took in marriage Caesar's sister Octavia. Quintus Salvidienus, who had set on foot wicked schemes against Caesar, he brought to light by his own information; and Salvidienus, being condemned, took his own life. Publius Ventidius, legate of Antonius, conquered the Parthians in battle and drove them from Syria, their leader Labienus being killed. When Sextus Pompeius, an enemy near to Italy, held Sicily and impeded the supply of grain, Caesar and Antonius made the peace he demanded with him, on condition that he should hold the province of Sicily. Besides this, the book contains disturbances in Africa and wars waged there.

title: Ab Urbe Condita (Periochae)
text:
128. When Sextus Pompeius again rendered the sea unsafe by piracies and did not keep the peace he had accepted, Caesar of necessity undertook war against him, and fought two naval battles with doubtful outcome. Publius Ventidius, legate of Marcus Antonius, conquered the Parthians in Syria in battle and killed their king. The Jews also were subdued by the legates of Antonius. Besides this, the book contains the preparation of the Sicilian war.
129. Against Sextus Pompeius operations were carried on with varying outcome in naval battles, so that of Caesar's two fleets the one, which Agrippa commanded, conquered, while the other, which Caesar had led, being destroyed, the soldiers set ashore were in great peril. Then Pompeius, defeated, fled into Sicily. Marcus Lepidus, who had crossed from Africa as though to a partnership in the war waged against Sextus Pompeius by Caesar, when he made war on Caesar too, being abandoned by his army, the honour of the triumvirate being annulled, obtained his life. Marcus Agrippa was presented with the naval crown by Caesar, an honour which had been paid to no one before him.
130. Marcus Antonius, while he revelled with Cleopatra, having tardily entered Media, made war on the Parthians with eighteen legions and sixteen thousand horse; and when, two legions being lost and nothing turning out prosperously, he was retreating, the Parthians pursuing again and again, with great trepidation and great peril to the whole army he returned into Armenia, having traversed in flight three hundred miles in twenty-one days. About eight thousand men he lost to storms. Storms also hostile to him, on top of a Parthian war so unhappily undertaken, he suffered by his own fault, because he was unwilling to winter in Armenia, while he hastened to Cleopatra.
131. Sextus Pompeius, when he came into the protection of Marcus Antonius, setting on foot war against him in Asia, was overpowered by his legates and killed, in the eighth year of his leadership. Caesar restrained a mutiny of the veterans, stirred up with great destruction, and subdued the Iapydes and the Dalmatians and the Pannonians. Antonius ordered Artavasdes, king of Armenia, brought to him under safe-conduct, to be thrown into chains, and gave the kingdom of Armenia to his own son born of Cleopatra, whom, long since captivated by love of her, he had begun to treat as a wife.
132. Caesar in Illyricum subdued the Dalmatians. When Marcus Antonius, on account of his love of Cleopatra, by whom he had two sons, Philadelphus and Alexander, would neither come to the city nor, the time of the triumvirate being finished, lay down his command, but was setting on foot a war to make on the city and Italy, vast forces both naval and land being gathered for this purpose, and a divorce being sent to Octavia, Caesar's sister, Caesar crossed into Epirus with an army. Then the naval battles and cavalry engagements favourable to Caesar are reported.
133. Marcus Antonius, defeated at Actium in a naval battle, fled to Alexandria; and besieged by Caesar, in the utmost despair of his affairs, driven especially by a false report of Cleopatra's death, killed himself. Caesar, Alexandria being reduced into his power, and Cleopatra, that she might not come into the power of the victor, having ended her life by voluntary death, returned into the city and held three triumphs, one over Illyricum, the second over the Actian victory, the third over Cleopatra, an end being imposed on the civil wars in the twenty-second year. Marcus Lepidus, son of the Lepidus who had been triumvir, having formed a conspiracy against Caesar and being about to set on foot war, was overpowered and killed.

title: Ab Urbe Condita (Periochae)
text:
134. Gaius Caesar, affairs being settled and all the provinces reduced to a fixed form, was also surnamed Augustus; and the month Sextilis was called in his honour. When he held an assembly at Narbo, a census was taken of the three Gauls, which Caesar his father had conquered. The war against the Bastarnae and the Moesi and other nations by Marcus Crassus . . . is reported.
135. The war waged by Marcus Crassus against the Thracians and by Caesar against the Spaniards is reported, and the Salassi, an Alpine people, were thoroughly subdued.
136. . . .
137. . . .
138. The Raeti were subdued by Tiberius Nero and Drusus, stepsons of Caesar. Agrippa, son-in-law of Caesar, died. A census was conducted by Drusus.
139. The states of Germany situated on this side of the Rhine and beyond the Rhine were assaulted by Drusus, and the disturbance which had arisen in Gaul over the census was composed. An altar of the deified Caesar was dedicated at the confluence of the Saône and the Rhone, Gaius Julius Vercondaridubnus the Aeduan being created its priest.
140. The Thracians subdued by Lucius Piso, and likewise the Cherusci, the Tencteri, the Chauci, and other nations of the Germans beyond the Rhine subdued by Drusus, are reported. Octavia, sister of Augustus, died, having earlier lost her son Marcellus; whose monuments are a theatre and a portico dedicated in his name.
141. The war waged against the nations beyond the Rhine by Drusus is reported, in which, among the foremost, Chumstinctus and Avectius, tribunes from the state of the Nervii, fought. Nero, brother of Drusus, subdued the Dalmatians and the Pannonians. Peace was made with the Parthians, the standards which had been captured under Crassus and afterwards under Antonius being returned by their king.
142. The war waged against the states of the Germans beyond the Rhine by Drusus is reported. He himself, from a fracture, his horse having collapsed upon his leg, died on the thirtieth day after it happened. His body was carried to Rome by his brother Nero, who, summoned by news of his illness, had hurried at full speed, and was laid in the tomb of Gaius Julius. He was eulogised by Caesar Augustus, his stepfather, and many further honours were paid to his memory.
